title: MongoDB and Redis
seriesDescription: Schema design and Postgres, scaling and multi-tenancy, MongoDB and Redis, consistency, warehouses and vector search. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Document modelling, indexes and aggregation pipelines in MongoDB, then Redis data types, TTL, eviction, caching patterns, stampedes and the limits of distributed locks.
source: MongoDB manual (aggregation, indexes, TTL, transactions); Redis docs (data types, eviction, persistence, distributed locks, ZRANGE/ZREVRANGE); Kleppmann on Redlock

questions.prompt: Which workload is the strongest case for choosing MongoDB over PostgreSQL?

options.text: Product catalogue with varied, evolving attributes per category.
options.why: Right: variable shape and read-the-whole-aggregate access fit the document model.

options.text: Double-entry ledger that needs many cross-table constraints, joins and strict audits.
options.why: Heavily relational integrity and joins are PostgreSQL strengths.

options.text: Ad-hoc analytical reporting across a dozen joined tables.
options.why: A warehouse or relational engine is a better fit than a document store.

options.text: A small reference table of 50 country codes.
options.why: Any store works; this is not a reason to introduce MongoDB.

questions.explanation: Pick Mongo for flexible schema, document-shaped aggregates and easy horizontal sharding. Pick SQL for strong relational integrity, complex joins and mature transactions. Mongo has multi-document transactions, but they cost more than single-document writes.

questions.prompt: Match each MongoDB index type with what it does.

left.text: Multikey index on a tags array

right.text: Serves equality on status and results sorted by createdAt
Creates one index key per array element
Lets the server delete documents once they are old enough
Indexes only the documents that match a filter, saving space
Indexes GeoJSON points on a sphere

questions.explanation: Compound indexes follow the equality, sort, range (ESR) guideline. A multikey index is automatic on array fields (a compound index may include at most one array field). TTL deletion runs in a background task about once a minute.

questions.prompt: Collection `orders` has documents `{customerId, status, amount}`. In mongosh, write `db.orders.aggregate(...)` returning the 3 customers with the highest total amount among orders whose status is "paid", as `{_id: customerId, total: ...}`.
questions.explanation: Put `$match` first so it can use an index and shrink the stream. `$sort` followed by `$limit` is optimised into a top-k sort. Quoting the stage keys (as JSON) is equally valid.

questions.prompt: Collection `orders` has documents `{customerId, status, amount}`. In mongosh, write a `find` that returns only `customerId` and `amount` (no `_id`) of the 5 largest orders whose status is "paid".
questions.explanation: The second argument of `find` is the projection; `_id` is returned unless excluded explicitly. The cursor methods `sort` and `limit` may be chained in any order because the server always applies sort, then skip, then limit. An aggregate with `$match`, `$sort`, `$limit` and `$project` is an equally valid answer.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: In MongoDB the order lines of an order are usually embedded inside the order document when they are always read together with it.
questions.reason: One read then returns the whole aggregate without a join or a second round trip, and a single-document write is atomic.

whys.a: Correct: co-located data means one read and one atomic write, which is why embedding is preferred.
whys.b: R is the reason, not just a true remark.

questions.explanation: Embed for one-to-few, read-together, bounded data. Reference when the child is large, unbounded, shared or updated independently (the 16 MB document limit is a hard stop).

questions.prompt: Collection `sales` holds `{sku:"a",qty:2}`, `{sku:"a",qty:3}`, `{sku:"b",qty:1}`, `{sku:"c",qty:6}`. The pipeline is `[{$group:{_id:"$sku", total:{$sum:"$qty"}}}, {$match:{total:{$gte:5}}}]`. How many documents does it output?
questions.explanation: Totals are a=5, b=1, c=6. Matching `total >= 5` keeps a and c, so 2. `$match` after `$group` is like `HAVING`.

questions.prompt: Match each Redis data structure with its natural use.

right.text: Object with fields, read with `HGET` and `HGETALL`
Leaderboard ranked by score with `ZADD` and `ZREVRANGE`
Durable append-only log read by consumer groups

questions.explanation: The last item is a HyperLogLog (`PFADD`, `PFCOUNT`), about 12 KB per key with roughly 0.81 percent standard error. A Redis list is fine for a queue but has no acknowledgement; streams add consumer groups and `XACK`. `ZREVRANGE` has been deprecated since Redis 6.2 in favour of `ZRANGE key 0 -1 REV`, but still works.

questions.prompt: Write the `redis-cli` command that stores the value `u1` under the key `session:abc` only if the key does not exist yet, and makes it expire after 60 seconds, in a single atomic command.

checks.label: uses SET on session:abc with value u1

questions.model: redis-cli SET session:abc u1 NX EX 60
questions.explanation: `SETNX` followed by `EXPIRE` is two commands, so a crash between them leaves a key that never expires. `SET` with `NX` and `EX` is atomic. The same pattern with a random token is the basis of a simple lock.

questions.prompt: Starting with no key `c`, `redis-cli` runs: `SET c 5`, then `INCRBY c 7`, then `DECR c`, then `INCR c`, then `INCR c`. What does `GET c` return?
questions.explanation: 5 + 7 = 12, `DECR` gives 11, then two `INCR`s give 13. These commands are atomic integer operations on a string value, which is why `INCR` is the standard counter and rate-limit primitive.

questions.prompt: Redis is used purely as a cache with `maxmemory` set. Every key is a rebuildable cache entry and many have no TTL. Which `maxmemory-policy` is the sensible choice?

options.why: Right: any key may be evicted, least recently used first, so writes keep succeeding.
Writes return OOM errors once memory is full, which is right for a primary store but not a cache.
Only keys with a TTL are candidates, so keys without TTL fill memory and writes can still fail.
Same candidate pool as `volatile-lru`, and it evicts by shortest remaining TTL, not usage.

questions.explanation: `allkeys-lfu` is the other good cache choice when frequency matters more than recency. Memory behaviour is a deployment decision that interviewers like to probe.

questions.text: In {1} the application checks the cache, loads from the database on a miss and then populates the cache; in {2} every write goes through the cache to the database synchronously; in {3} writes hit the cache first and are flushed to the database later.
questions.explanation: Cache-aside is the default pattern: the application owns the lookup and the fill. Write-behind is fastest but can lose acknowledged writes if the cache dies before the flush.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Adding random jitter to cache TTLs reduces the chance of many hot keys expiring at the same instant.
questions.reason: Jitter makes cache entries never expire, so the database is never queried again.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Correct: jitter spreads expiry times (A true); entries still expire (R false).

questions.explanation: Stampede defences: jitter, single-flight or a per-key mutex so only one caller recomputes, serving stale while revalidating, and probabilistic early refresh.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Redis-based distributed locks are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: A lock without an expiry is held forever if its owner crashes.
options.why: Right: `SET ... NX PX ttl` exists to avoid this.

options.text: Unlock must verify the stored token and delete atomically, for example with a Lua script.
options.why: Right: otherwise you can delete a lock another client acquired after yours expired.

options.text: A paused holder (GC, network stall) can act after its lock expired, so the resource should check a fencing token.
options.why: Right: the expiry cannot stop a client that does not know it lost the lock.

options.text: One Redis instance with `SET NX EX` guarantees mutual exclusion even through failover.
options.why: With asynchronous replication a failover can promote a replica that never saw the key.

options.text: Redlock is accepted by all experts as safe for correctness-critical locking.
options.why: Martin Kleppmann disputed its timing assumptions; use it for efficiency, not correctness.

questions.explanation: Rule of thumb: Redis locks are fine for efficiency (avoid duplicate work). For correctness use a fencing token or a consensus system such as ZooKeeper or etcd.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: A Redis `SET NX PX` lock can still be held by two clients at once in some failure cases.
questions.reason: Redis executes commands on a single thread.

whys.a: Single-threaded execution does not stop duplicate holders after expiry or failover.
whys.b: Correct: both true, but atomic command execution is not the cause of the failure cases.

questions.explanation: Single-threaded execution makes each command atomic. The failures come from expiry during a pause and asynchronous replication, not from interleaved commands.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Deleting the cache entry before the database transaction commits is safe against stale reads.
questions.reason: A concurrent reader that misses the cache can reload the old row between the delete and the commit.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot be explaining a true statement.
whys.b: A is false: deleting early leaves a window in which stale data is re-cached.
whys.c: R is true, so the option calling it false is wrong.
whys.d: Correct: the reader repopulates the cache with the old row before the commit lands, so the stale value then lives until the TTL; R is true.

questions.explanation: Invalidate after the commit (and keep a TTL as a safety net), or use delayed double delete or change-data-capture driven invalidation. Invalidating early is a classic cache-aside race.

questions.prompt: True or false: MongoDB has no multi-document transactions, so atomic updates must always be modelled inside a single document.

options.why: Right: replica sets support multi-document ACID transactions since 4.0 and sharded clusters since 4.2.

questions.explanation: Single-document atomicity is still the preferred design because it avoids transaction overhead, but transactions exist when you need them.

questions.prompt: Complete the compound-index rule of thumb.
questions.text: Order the fields of a compound index as {1} first, then {2}, then {3} (the ESR guideline).
questions.explanation: Equality fields narrow to an exact key prefix, sort fields then deliver ordered output without an in-memory sort, and range fields come last because a range on an earlier field breaks the ordering of later ones. So `find({status:'paid', amount:{$gt:10}}).sort({createdAt:-1})` is served best by `{status:1, createdAt:-1, amount:1}`.

questions.prompt: Match each Redis persistence option with its trait.

right.text: Compact point-in-time file; a crash loses writes since the last snapshot
Command log fsynced each second; at most about one second of writes can be lost
Command log fsynced on every write; safest and slowest
Pure in-memory cache; a restart starts empty
Synchronous replication to every replica before replying

questions.explanation: RDB is good for backups and fast restarts; AOF trades speed for durability, and everysec is the default fsync policy. Redis replication is asynchronous by default, so neither option makes Redis a strongly consistent store (WAIT narrows but does not close that gap).
